fields.definition: A subjective timbral descriptor for a rough, buzzy, low-pitched and harmonically dense tone with an aggressive, gritty character. On wind and brass instruments 'growl' also names a specific technique in which the player hums or sings while blowing, producing rough beating overtones against the sounded note.
fields.plain_english: A growl is a rough, buzzy, low sound, like a big animal grumbling. On a sax, players make it by humming while they blow, which roughs up the note.
fields.purpose_function: The label lets engineers and players quickly aim for and describe a gritty, aggressive low-end character during tracking, mixing, or sound design.
fields.practical_application: An engineer might add saturation, mild distortion, or a resonant low-mid boost to make a bass or synth sound growly, or close-mic a saxophone's bell to capture a played growl.
common_mistakes: Confusing growl with plain distortion, when growl specifically implies a rough, low, buzzy quality rather than any harmonic clipping.
Assuming a saxophone growl is added in the mix, when it is actually a live playing technique.
Over-adding low-mid saturation until the tone becomes muddy rather than growly.
scenario_contexts: Describing a distorted bass guitar tone in a mix note.
A saxophonist adding growl to a solo in a jazz or funk chart.
Sound-designing an aggressive synth bass for electronic music.

sources: The New Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments
Baines, Woodwind Instruments and Their History
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers

fields.definition: The initial percussive transient of a struck-string instrument such as a piano, produced at the moment the felt-covered hammer strikes the strings, before the note settles into its sustained, harmonically rich decay.
fields.plain_english: The sharp start of a piano note, made when the hammer hits the strings. It is the quick 'thock' you hear just before the note rings out.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a piano note its clear, percussive onset, which helps the ear place the note in time and recognize the instrument.
fields.practical_application: When close-miking a piano, a technician balances mic position and transient handling so the hammer attack stays crisp without sounding clicky.
common_mistakes: Confusing the hammer attack (the musical transient) with mechanical hammer noise (unwanted action sound).
Over-compressing the attack until the piano loses its natural percussive punch.
Placing the mic so far back that the attack goes soft and undefined.
scenario_contexts: Setting a compressor's attack time so a piano's initial transient is not squashed.
Choosing a sample library based on how realistic its hammer attack sounds.
EQ-ing a pop piano so the attack cuts through a dense mix.

sources: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber and Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: The soft, non-tonal component of a piano note's onset caused by the felt of the hammer compressing against the strings, heard as a cushioned thud layered under the pitched attack. Its character depends on felt hardness, wear, and voicing.
fields.plain_english: The soft, dull sound the fuzzy hammer felt makes as it hits the piano strings. It is the padded thump mixed into the note's start.
fields.purpose_function: It is a natural part of a real piano's tone, and its softness or hardness is shaped by voicing the felt to make the instrument brighter or mellower.
fields.practical_application: A technician may notice heavy felt noise on a close-miked piano and adjust mic placement, or a piano technician may voice or reshape worn felt to control it.
common_mistakes: Mistaking normal felt noise for a mechanical fault.
Trying to remove felt noise entirely with EQ, which thins the natural attack.
Ignoring hardened, worn felt that has made the noise harsh and clicky.
scenario_contexts: Recording a soft solo piano passage where felt noise becomes noticeable.
A piano technician voicing hammers to reduce a hard, noisy felt strike.
Editing a close-miked piano track to tame distracting attack noise.

sources: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber and Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: Non-tonal mechanical sound generated by a piano's hammer and action striking the strings, distinct from the pitched tone; it includes felt contact, wood knock, and action movement, and is heard mainly at the note's onset.
fields.plain_english: The mechanical clunk of the piano's moving parts as a key is played, apart from the musical note. It is the 'machine' sound of the hammer hitting.
fields.purpose_function: In small amounts it adds realism and presence to a piano's attack, but heavy hammer noise usually signals worn parts or poor voicing.
fields.practical_application: When close-miking a piano, a technician sets mic distance and levels so hammer noise stays natural rather than distractingly loud.
common_mistakes: Assuming all hammer noise is a defect rather than a normal part of piano tone.
Placing mics right over the hammers, which exaggerates the noise.
Confusing hammer noise with string buzz or pedal noise.
scenario_contexts: Diagnosing loud mechanical noise on a close-miked grand piano.
A technician judging whether hammer noise points to worn felt.
Choosing mic distance to balance tone against action noise.

sources: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber and Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: The physical event in which a piano hammer contacts the string or strings, imparting energy that sets them vibrating; it is the excitation that begins each note.
fields.plain_english: The moment the piano hammer actually hits the strings and makes them ring. It is what starts every piano note.
fields.purpose_function: It is the mechanism that turns a key press into sound, transferring the player's energy into string vibration.
fields.practical_application: Understanding the hammer strike helps a technician judge attack character and diagnose issues like double-striking or uneven tone across keys.
common_mistakes: Confusing the hammer strike (the physical event) with the hammer attack (the resulting sound).
Overlooking a hammer that strikes twice and causes a stuttered note.
Assuming a harder key press changes only loudness, when it also changes strike tone.
scenario_contexts: Explaining why velocity changes both level and timbre in a piano sample.
A technician regulating the action so each hammer strikes cleanly.
Analyzing the onset of a piano note for sample editing.

sources: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers

fields.definition: A dull, low-frequency thud in a struck-instrument onset produced by the mass of the hammer contacting the sounding element, heard as a soft low knock beneath the pitched attack.
fields.plain_english: A low, soft thump at the start of a note when the hammer hits. It is the deep knock you feel more than hear.
fields.purpose_function: It adds weight and body to the attack, but too much can muddy the low end or mask the note's pitch.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may use a high-pass filter or transient control to tame an excessive hammer thump on a close-miked piano or mallet instrument.
common_mistakes: Confusing musical low-end body with unwanted hammer thump.
High-passing so hard that the instrument loses its natural weight.
Blaming the room for a thump that is actually mechanical.
scenario_contexts: Cleaning up a boomy close-miked piano recording.
Taming low thump on a mallet percussion track.
Setting a high-pass filter on a piano channel in a live mix.

sources: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber and Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques

fields.definition: A performance artifact consisting of the incidental sound made when a player moves or resets a hand on an instrument, such as fingers shifting on a fretboard, string bed, or keys, captured as a brief non-musical noise between or during notes.
fields.plain_english: The little noise a player makes when they move a hand to a new spot on an instrument. Think of fingers sliding to a new place on guitar strings.
fields.purpose_function: Recognizing it helps an engineer decide whether the noise is natural performance detail worth keeping or a distraction to edit out.
fields.practical_application: During editing, a technician may fade, mute, or lightly EQ a hand-reposition noise so it does not distract in an exposed passage.
common_mistakes: Removing every reposition noise, which can make a recording sound lifeless and unnatural.
Missing loud reposition noises in quiet, exposed sections.
Confusing a hand-reposition noise with a mechanical instrument fault.
scenario_contexts: Editing finger-slide noise on a solo acoustic guitar track.
Cleaning up an exposed harp or piano passage.
Deciding how much natural handling noise to keep for realism.

sources: Huber and Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers

fields.definition: A convex steel percussion instrument (an idiophone) formed from two joined hemispherical shells, with a central tuned note and a surrounding ring of tuned tone fields hammered into the top surface, played with the hands and fingers. It descends from the Hang, which was developed using steelpan tuning techniques.
fields.plain_english: A rounded steel drum played with the hands, shaped a bit like a flying saucer. Tapping its dented spots gives soft, bell-like notes.
fields.purpose_function: It produces gentle, sustaining, harmonically rich tones for melodic and rhythmic playing without sticks, filling a mellow tuned-percussion role.
fields.practical_application: When recording a handpan, an engineer usually uses one or two condenser mics to capture its wide tuned resonance and long sustain while controlling room reflections.
common_mistakes: Calling every handpan a 'Hang', which is one specific maker's trademarked instrument.
Miking too close, which loses the instrument's blended overtones and sustain.
Expecting steel-drum brightness when the handpan is far mellower.
scenario_contexts: Recording a handpan for ambient or meditative music.
Placing mics to capture its long, ringing sustain in a live set.
Blending a handpan with soft percussion in a mix.

sources: Fletcher and Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
The New Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments

fields.definition: An onset with a fast, sharp, high-energy transient in which a note reaches full level almost immediately, giving a percussive, aggressive character. It contrasts with a soft or slow attack that fades in gradually.
fields.plain_english: A note that starts fast and sharp, hitting full volume right away. Think of slapping a drum instead of gently blowing a flute.
fields.purpose_function: A hard attack helps a sound cut through a mix and read as punchy or percussive, which aids rhythm and clarity.
fields.practical_application: A technician can create or keep a hard attack by setting a synth's amp envelope to a near-zero attack time, or by using a slower compressor attack that lets the transient through.
common_mistakes: Setting a fast compressor attack that clamps the transient and softens the intended hard attack.
Confusing a hard attack (fast onset) with high overall loudness.
Adding a click transient so sharp it distorts or tires the listener.
scenario_contexts: Programming a plucky synth bass with an instant attack.
Dialing compressor attack time to keep a snare's hard hit.
Describing a percussive piano or mallet sound in a session note.

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers
Huber and Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques
